notes.title: Quantum Mechanics Basics
notes.content:
These are my notes on quantum mechanics. The fundamental principle is that energy is discrete. We talked about the Schrödinger equation, which governs how the quantum state of a physical system changes over time.

Wave-particle duality is a key concept, meaning that every particle or quantum entity may be described as either a particle or a wave.

Here is some more content to ensure the text overflows and the show more button appears. We also learned about Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, which states that we cannot know both the exact position and momentum of a particle at the same time.

notes.title: The Industrial Revolution
notes.content:
Started in Great Britain in the late 18th century. Transition to new manufacturing processes.

Key inventions:

  1. Spinning Jenny
  2. Steam Engine
  3. Power Loom

It brought about massive social and economic changes, moving people from rural areas to urban centers.

notes.title: Analysis of '1984'
notes.content:
George Orwell's dystopian novel explores themes of totalitarianism, mass surveillance, and repressive regimentation. The concept of Doublethink and Newspeak are particularly relevant.

"War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength."

notes.title: Cellular Respiration
notes.content:
The process by which biological fuels are oxidized in the presence of an inorganic electron acceptor to produce large amounts of energy, to drive the bulk production of ATP.

Stages:

  • Glycolysis
  • Krebs Cycle
  • Electron Transport Chain

notes.title: Cell Division: Mitosis vs Meiosis
notes.content:
Mitosis: somatic cells, 1 division, 2 identical diploid daughter cells.
Meiosis: sex cells (gametes), 2 divisions, 4 genetically different haploid cells.

notes.title: Thermodynamics Laws
notes.content:
• 0th Law: Thermal equilibrium.
  • 1st Law: Energy cannot be created or destroyed (conservation of energy).
  • 2nd Law: Entropy of an isolated system always increases.
  • 3rd Law: Entropy approaches a constant value as temperature approaches absolute zero.

notes.title: Functional Groups Summary
notes.content: Alcohols (-OH), Aldehydes (-CHO), Ketones (C=O), Carboxylic Acids (-COOH), Amines (-NH2). Knowing these is crucial for predicting chemical reactions.

notes.title: Data Structures: Hash Tables
notes.content: Provides O(1) average time complexity for lookups, insertions, and deletions. Uses a hash function to map keys to indices in an array. Collisions can be handled via chaining or open addressing.

notes.title: Comprehensive Guide to System Design
notes.content:
Introduction to System Design

System design is the process of defining the architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data for a system to satisfy specified requirements. Systems design could be seen as the application of systems theory to product development.

Key Characteristics

  • Scalability: The capability of a system to handle a growing amount of work, or its potential to be enlarged to accommodate that growth.
  • Reliability: The probability a system will fail in a given period. In distributed systems, this is often achieved through redundancy.
  • Availability: The time a system remains operational to perform its required function in a specific period. Usually measured in nines (e.g., 99.999%).
  • Efficiency: Two standard measures are response time (latency) and throughput (bandwidth).
  • Maintainability: How easily a system can be modified to correct faults, improve performance, or adapt to a changed environment.

Load Balancing

A load balancer is a critical component of any distributed system. It helps to spread the traffic across a cluster of servers to improve responsiveness and availability of applications, websites or databases.

Load Balancing Algorithms

  1. Round Robin: Requests are distributed across the group of servers sequentially.
  2. Least Connections: A new request is sent to the server with the fewest current connections to clients.
  3. Least Response Time: Directs traffic to the server with the fewest active connections and the lowest average response time.
  4. IP Hash: The IP address of the client is used to determine which server receives the request.

Caching

Caching enables you to make vastly better use of the resources you already have. Caches take advantage of the locality of reference principle: recently requested data is likely to be requested again. They are used in almost every layer of computing: hardware, operating systems, web browsers, web applications, and more.

By storing frequently accessed data in a fast, temporary storage layer (like RAM), we can drastically reduce the latency of subsequent requests and alleviate load on the primary database.

Cache Eviction Policies

  • First In First Out (FIFO): The cache evicts the first block accessed first without any regard to how often or how many times it was accessed before.
  • Last In First Out (LIFO): The cache evicts the block accessed most recently first without any regard to how often or how many times it was accessed before.
  • Least Recently Used (LRU): Discards the least recently used items first. This is the most popular caching strategy.
  • Least Frequently Used (LFU): Counts how often an item is needed. Those that are used least often are discarded first.

Database Partitioning (Sharding)

Data partitioning (also known as sharding) is a technique to break up a big database into many smaller parts. It is the process of splitting up a DB/table across multiple machines to improve the manageability, performance, availability, and load balancing of an application.

As the application scales, a single database might not be enough to handle the sheer volume of data or the high read/write throughput. Sharding solves this by horizontally partitioning the data.
